MoofTCP – A modern replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:54:15 UTC
09:54:15 KST

A modern, memory-lean replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs running System 6.
MoofTCP is a drop-in replacement for Apple's MacTCP. Programs written for MacTCP run on it unchanged, but underneath it is a fresh TCP/IP stack written from scratch in portable C, with its own control panel, installer and DHCP client. It was built for a Mac Classic with 4 MB of RAM, so every byte counts.
MacTCP is wonderful, but it is old, and on a 4 MB Mac Classic with a SCSI Wi-Fi/Ethernet adapter like BlueSCSI it can be slow to answer, hungry for memory, and awkward to set up. MoofTCP aims, in this order, for:
- Reliability. No hangs, no leaks, no surprises when apps quit.
- Low latency for interactive use, like typing in a telnet session.
- Throughput, for handling quasi-modern use cases.
...all while using no more resident memory than MacTCP does.
- Drop-in compatible. Implements the MacTCP .IPP driver interface (TCP, UDP, ICMP echo) and the dnrp name resolver. Your existing MacTCP programs just work.
- DHCP or a fixed address. Pick either in the control panel. Don't need to manage static IP anymore.
- MoofTCP Lite. A build without DHCP that saves about 5 KB of system memory, for tight machines. One installer holds both; a checkbox picks which one.
- A friendly installer. It moves MacTCP's files aside, installs MoofTCP, and its Remove button puts everything back exactly as it was. An interrupted install repairs itself.
- MultiFinder-aware. Quitting an app that had connections open cleans up after it.
- Built-in diagnostics. An optional in-memory log and a small MoofDiag tool for bug reports.
- A portable core. The TCP/IP stack in core/ has no malloc and no global state, and is tested on the
desktop with sanitizers and fuzzers.
- Download MoofTCP-1.0.dsk, MoofTCP-1.0.hqx or MoofTCP-1.0.sit from the
Releases page and get it onto your Mac (a BlueSCSI shared folder works well).
- Open MoofTCP Installer, leave Lite version (no DHCP) unticked, and click Install.
- Restart the Mac.
- Open Control Panels, MoofTCP, enter your IP address, mask, router and DNS server (or tick Get the address by DHCP), and save.
- Restart again. You're online.
To go back to MacTCP, run the installer and click Remove. The Read Me file in the release has the
details, including how to switch between MoofTCP and MoofTCP Lite.
StuffIt Lite 3.6 is tested as working for expanding the .hqx packages.
- A 68k Mac with System 6.0.8 (the version it was tested on). Please report back if it works on other versions!
- An Ethernet adapter that provides the .ENET0 driver, such as a BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT. MoofTCP
does not include an Ethernet driver.
Tested on a real Mac Classic (System 6.0.8, 4 MB, BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT) and in the Snow emulator.
Have a program that doesn't work? Please open an issue (see below).
MultiFinder grows the system heap on demand, so free memory varies more there.
MoofTCP keeps a small diagnostic log in memory. If a program misbehaves but the Mac keeps running, run
MoofDiag right away (it is in the release's diagnostic tools download), and open an issue with the
MoofDiag.out file it writes next to itself, plus a note about what you were doing. Feel free to ask your LLM
to analyze the codebase and the diagnostic output as well and to submit fix PRs.
- No IPv6.
- Tested only with the DaynaPORT Ethernet driver on System 6.0.8.
- DHCP is basic: no lease RELEASE, no INIT-REBOOT and no address-conflict probe. While it runs, programs cannot use UDP port 68. With no DHCP server, the first open waits about 10 seconds and then fails.
You only need Docker. The pinned Retro68 cross-compiler image is pulled automatically.
scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP              # the MoofTCP file -> build-mac/moof/
MT_LITE=1 scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP    # MoofTCP Lite -> build-mac-lite/
scripts/release.sh --force 1.0            # one installer with both -> dist/MoofTCP-1.0.{dsk,hqx,sit}
release.sh also needs hfsutils, macutils, unar, gcc and Python 3.
The portable core and the glue logic are tested on your desktop with gcc and CMake (AddressSanitizer and UBSan are on by default):
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
cmake -S . -B build-lite -DMT_NO_DHCP=ON   # the Lite configuration
The emulator tests (Snow) need Apple system software and the BlueSCSI DaynaPORT image. Those are not in this
repository and you must supply them yourself; the scripts in scripts/ (setup-home.sh, golden-stage.sh) show
what is expected.
core/      portable TCP/IP stack (no malloc, no globals), host-tested
mac/       Mac glue: .IPP driver, INIT, resolver, control panel, installer, diagnostic apps
tests/     host tests (ctest), including fuzzers
scripts/   build, release, emulator and hardware-session scripts
tools/     pinned tool versions; tools/sit is a small StuffIt-format writer
Bug reports, compatibility reports ("program X does/doesn't work") and pull requests are welcome. For code
changes, please read CONTRIBUTING.md and run the host tests first (see above). CLAUDE.md is a
detailed map of the code and its rules. Security problems: see SECURITY.md.
- Retro68 for the 68k cross-compiler.
- Snow for the Mac emulator the tests run in.
- BlueSCSI and DaynaPORT for the network hardware this was built around.
- Claude Code was used to develop this project, with human planning and testing.
- More comprehensive bake-in testing on real hardware as we use it
- Remake Daynaport similarly (stay tuned for MoofPort)
- Review the BlueSCSI codebase for opportunities to integrate more tightly for better performance
- There is potential for further algorithm optimization for added performance on smaller or older systems.
MIT. "MacTCP" and "StuffIt" are trademarks of their owners and are used here only to describe compatibility. MoofTCP contains no Apple or third-party code; building it uses Apple's interfaces as shipped in the Retro68 toolchain.

OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:37:56 UTC
09:37:56 KST

Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.
OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments.
Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.
OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

The New York Times reportedly in talks to buy Letterboxd for $330 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:07:18 UTC
09:07:18 KST

The New York Times Company has reportedly “entered exclusive negotiations” to acquire Letterboxd for $330 million, according to a report from The New York Times itself.
Letterboxd, an online platform for movie lovers that could be compared to Goodreads for movies, has grown dramatically in recent years. Letterboxd reported 3 million users in January 2021, a figure that grew to 28 million by April of this year. More than half of its users are under 35.
Letterboxd was previously reported to be seeking a new owner. According to the Times, film studios A24 and Sony were interested in the acquisition, but A24 was priced out.
Letterboxd is free, but users can access advanced features with a paid subscription. Its projected earnings for this year are estimated at $15 million, which is only about 4.5% of what the Times is supposedly offering to buy the company for.
The New York Times Company declined to comment on the acquisition to its own paper (lol). Personally, we wouldn’t be surprised if these anonymous tips were coming from inside the house, so we’re inclined to take this report pretty seriously.

Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:06:12 UTC
09:06:12 KST

Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter released today.
Airbnb is working on an AI travel agent
The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year.
“Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge.
Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work:
We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb.
Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said before that the company plans to launch an agent in 2027, telling the Skift Global Forum that it would have an interface that’s “much richer than a chatbot.”
In its shareholder letter, Airbnb also said that AI is “the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb” and has changed how it develops products and operates.

Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:01:38 UTC
09:01:38 KST

Meta, Google, and TikTok have each filed lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta in an attempt to block a law that restricts social media features it deems addictive for users under 16.
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill, known as AB 1709, into law in September, and it’s slated to take effect at the start of the new year.
The law prohibits social platforms from offering autoplay videos and personalized feeds to users under 16, and it requires the platforms to delete these users’ accounts if they don’t turn those features off. If platforms do not comply, they could be liable for fines of up to $50,000 per affected user under 16 years old.
Meta claims that AB 1709 violates the First Amendment by overriding its editorial decisions about how to display content, adding that Section 230 preempts the law. TikTok and Google made similar arguments.
“Meta currently organizes its feeds of content to include personalized content recommendations and to automatically play media, [so] the Act would make it unlawful for Meta to disseminate speech to minors altogether, and would require Meta to delete minors’ accounts, unless it changes these practices,” the company wrote in its lawsuit.
In an emailed statement, a TikTok spokesperson added, “AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use.”
AB 1709 follows a trend of legislation around the world that seeks to curb teen social media use in an attempt to improve teen mental health outcomes. However, digital safety experts often caution against these laws because they can inadvertently compromise the privacy of all platform users, including adults, by requiring age verification checks that collect more user data.
“AB 1709 compels platforms to collect even more information from every user, invading everyone’s privacy and frustrating our ability to remain anonymous online,” EFF Associate Director of State Affairs Rindala Alajaji said in a press briefing. “Online surveillance by social media companies is harmful, and yet this bill requires even more of it, further concentrating power in the hands of tech companies rather than actually protecting users.”
Alajaji added that teenagers’ use of social media has been instrumental in enabling impactful digital activism, citing the Parkland shooting survivors’ March for Our Lives and climate activist Greta Thunberg’s global reach.
“As a functional ban on social media for youth under 16, AB 1709 cuts young people off from essential information and experiences, silencing the very voices it claims to protect,” Alajaji said.
These platforms are primed to fight this California law as they navigate similar legal battles in various countries. That’s especially true for Meta, which agreed to pay a settlement of up to $18 billion to resolve children’s safety claims brought by 29 U.S. states.
In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban social media for users under 16 altogether. France passed a similar law, but its top court struck it down, citing concerns about violations of free expression rights.
These platforms also argue that the law would affect parents’ ability to make decisions about their teens’ internet use through parental controls.
A Google spokesperson noted that autoplay on YouTube is turned off for minors by default, and that parents have the ability to turn off their teens’ access to Shorts altogether.
“We believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,” a Google spokesperson said. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
A representative for Attorney General Bonta said that his office is reviewing the filings and is committed to “defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

Inkling 2 Small
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
00:00:24 UTC
09:00:24 KST

Today we are introducing our second model generation with Inkling 2 Small. It is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters, 17B active, and supports image inputs and variable effort.
Inkling 2 Small far surpasses our previous models’ scores on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 31, reflecting gains in performance on agentic coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning. The increase in capabilities comes from improvements made at every step of our training process, including more efficient pre-training and a large, unified RL run.
Inkling 2 Small will initially be available through Tinker, with closed weights, following the approach we outlined in a safe path to open weights. We intend to make the full weights available under an Apache 2.0 license next week after the completion of external safety testing and red-teaming.
You can try Inkling 2 Small on Tinker Playground today. The model is also available for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker; checkpoints will be downloadable with the release of Inkling 2 Small’s weights.
Capabilities
Inkling 2 Small is more capable across the board than our first generation, particularly in long-horizon autonomous work.
Inkling 2 Small’s vision and agentic capabilities enable it to incorporate visual feedback to iteratively build and refine websites, games, and 3D designs with interactive elements.
Agentic coding and autoresearch
Inkling 2 Small was trained with RL on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks across multiple agent harnesses and context-compaction strategies. We increased the quality of our synthetic coding data pipeline and moved beyond unit-test rewards alone; many tasks included an agentic RL grader that evaluated how the model approached the problem, not just whether its code passed. We also tested early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small on OpenCode under the name Fledge-Alpha to assess our model’s performance on coding tasks in the real world.
The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops. Inkling 2 Small improves on usability compared to Inkling: it follows instructions better, considers changes carefully, and verifies its work without being asked.
Beyond conventional software tasks, Inkling 2 Small was also trained on long-horizon autoresearch tasks. This included agentic GPU kernel optimization and ML tasks such as post-training a model autonomously, all run across a range of GPU architectures.
To demonstrate its end-to-end autoresearch performance, we tested Inkling 2 Small on a task Proximal built for one of our internal benchmarks. Inkling 2 Small autonomously trained Qwen3.5-4B on Tinker to predict various time series such as weather and Wikipedia page views. It started by analyzing the tasks and writing its own evaluator, experimented with training datasets and recipes, and tried various approaches to SFT and RL, while debugging the process as it goes. After 4.5 hours of work and $426 in Tinker spend, the trained model has more than doubled its forecasting score.
Vision interpretation and creation
Inkling 2 Small processes image inputs using a 292M-parameter vision encoder based on Perception EncoderBolya et al., 2025.. We use 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling, and interleave image patches with text tokens. The model demonstrates strong visual capabilities across multiple categories, including OCR, grounding, infographic interpretation, and visual reasoning.
The model uses vision in the loop to interpret and validate the visual coding output it generates. Pending the release of its weights, it is set to be the top open-weights model on DesignArena.
We even tested Inkling 2 Small against some of our researchers in a wine tasting event. It outperformed them using vision alone, correctly identifying three wines from a single picture in 19 out of 20 trials.
Agentic knowledge work
Inkling 2 Small accelerates knowledge work in realistic professional environments. It proficiently looks up information, calls tools over MCP, and produces high-quality deliverables. On AA-Briefcase, an end-to-end knowledge work benchmark, these capabilities come together for an ELO score of 1527.
Inkling 2 Small is especially strong in finance and quantitative reasoning over spreadsheets, filings and documents. Among open weight models, Inkling 2 Small is the best performing model across several finance benchmarks.
Customizability
Some models respond better to fine-tuning, independent of their out-of-the-box performance. We wanted Inkling 2 Small to be a strong base model for customization.
Inkling 2 Small learns faster and improves more than our previous models when trained on the same data and algorithm across a variety of post-training scenarios, which we curated based on customer use cases. For example, starting from similarly low scores on a public financial-document summarization task, Inkling 2 Small adapts quickly, reaching the final performance of Inkling Small with just 75 training steps and finishing substantially ahead.
Reasoning, knowledge, and epistemics
Inkling 2 Small is trained on challenging STEM problems, instruction following, information seeking with and without web search, and forecasting tasks. During RL, we use proper scoring rules for forecasting tasks and uncertainty-sensitive rewards on some question-answering tasks. This trained the model to assess uncertainty, express appropriate confidence, and make well-calibrated predictions.
Safety and alignment
Our safety work for Inkling 2 Small centers on two questions: how the model performs for the general user, and how well it resists the removal of safeguards by a malicious actor. The release of Inkling’s weights is pending further safety evaluations by us and our partners.
To assess misuse risks, we trained an internal helpful-only variant. We ran both this model and the release checkpoint through a wider suite of evaluations, with more external testers, than any previous release.
On chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risk, Inkling 2 Small’s knowledge and capability scores sit below the open-weight frontier. On FORTRESS, Scale AI’s private benchmark that scores how much harmful assistance a model gives in response to expert-written adversarial prompts across CBRN, terrorism, and nonviolent crime, Inkling 2 Small has a lower Average Risk Score compared with Inkling and Inkling-Small, and also demonstrates a higher Overrefusal Score (see Limitations). The helpful-only variant of Inkling 2 Small exhibits marginal uplift on CBRN knowledge relative to the release checkpoint, but it does not significantly advance the frontier on any dimension we measured.
On offensive and dual-use agentic cyber benchmarks, Inkling 2 Small is a large step up from Inkling Small but remains behind the open-weight frontier. It matches the open-weight frontier on Vals CyberBench v1.1 and PatchEval, both of which measure the ability to find and patch security vulnerabilities.
* While we handle mental distress situations well, our model sometimes overreacts with disclaimers in normal emotional support queries as mentioned in the Limitations section.
As models take on unsupervised, longer-horizon autonomous work, the potential harm from their misbehavior increases. Without proper attention to alignment, capabilities-focused RL can push models to succeed at any cost. When tasks were difficult, early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small were persistent in trying to succeed—in some cases fabricating results, ignoring instructions, and concealing what they had done.
We worked across the stack to improve model alignment. In midtraining, we filtered out traces containing misbehavior and included traces with honest, aligned behavior. In RL, we added a general alignment reward that penalizes misbehavior on every task. We also built environments targeting specific failure modes we observed in training, such as rewarding models for giving up on impossible tasks. Finally, we used on-policy self-distillationZhao et al., 2026. from a teacher model prompted with a conduct spec, so the model internalizes principles for good behavior without explicit prompting.
We measured progress with both internal and external evaluations, and found that Inkling 2 Small substantially improves over previous Inkling models on both internal and external evaluations, and outperforms a set of comparable open-weights models on our internal evals.
Inkling 2 Small still trails closed-weights models, such as GPT-6.1 Sol on our alignment evaluations. Reducing this gap is a priority for future models.
We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory.
Training Inkling 2 Small
Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon.
We followed this initial phase with a second phase (H2) of 3.8 trillion tokens of higher-quality, newer data the model hadn’t seen, at 512K context. The third and fourth phases mixed in data in the deployment format. The third phase was about 320 billion tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context, alongside replayed pretraining data. The fourth phase (H4) kept only the highest-quality data: about 34 billion tokens of agent trajectories. The H3 and H4 mixtures consisted mostly of trajectories sampled from earlier models including Kimi K3 and our own models, filtered for correctness and alignment.
We then carried out a joint RL run, consisting of 1,075 steps and over 17 million rollouts over 9 days. See table below for more details. This single joint run contrasts with the previous Inkling release, where we ran separate reasoning and agentic RL runs and combined them with multi-teacher distillation.
The task mix included software engineering in real repositories, terminal tasks, document creation, STEM question answering, vision, web app building, tool use with simulated users, and safety. Each task family had its own grader:
hidden unit tests and programmatic checks for most coding work;
rubric-based LLM judges for documents and tool use;
reference answers for STEM and vision question answering;
pairwise reward models comparing screenshots of rendered web apps.
We randomly sampled and conditioned on an effort level, and applied a length penalty in the reward function, which trained the model to trade off speed and thoroughness.
Our asynchronous RL uses a score centering variant—the StableReinforce objective in Tinker—which tolerates significant staleness. Our run combines short and long horizon tasks with p50/p99 total rollout tokens being 43k and 1.5M respectively and p50/p99 duration of 8 minutes and 4 hours respectively. We use 256k context length and enable compaction training for long-horizon tasks. As a result, both training reward and evaluation performance grow log-linearly with compute.
Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals.
Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above.
Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon.
Benchmarking Inkling 2 Small
Like previous Inkling releases, we benchmarked Inkling-Small on a broad range of capabilities. All evals run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. All evals run with a 1M-token maximum trajectory limit, increased from the 256K-token limit used for Inkling Small.
Highest reported score in each row; ties includedSecond-highest reported score in each row; ties included
Evaluation snapshot: Missing results are shown as dashes.
Limitations
While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills.
Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio.
Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries.
Try Inkling 2 Small today
We are proud to make Inkling 2 Small available on Tinker for inference and fine tuning. Following the completion of safety testing, the model will be available on additional platforms in the coming weeks.
Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. We hope that it encourages your ambitions, and we look forward to seeing what you build with it.

Agentic knowledge work
Inkling 2 Small accelerates knowledge work in realistic professional environments. It proficiently looks up information, calls tools over MCP, and produces high-quality deliverables. On AA-Briefcase, an end-to-end knowledge work benchmark, these capabilities come together for an ELO score of 1527.
Inkling 2 Small is especially strong in finance and quantitative reasoning over spreadsheets, filings and documents. Among open weight models, Inkling 2 Small is the best performing model across several finance benchmarks.
Customizability
Some models respond better to fine-tuning, independent of their out-of-the-box performance. We wanted Inkling 2 Small to be a strong base model for customization.
Inkling 2 Small learns faster and improves more than our previous models when trained on the same data and algorithm across a variety of post-training scenarios, which we curated based on customer use cases. For example, starting from similarly low scores on a public financial-document summarization task, Inkling 2 Small adapts quickly, reaching the final performance of Inkling Small with just 75 training steps and finishing substantially ahead.
Reasoning, knowledge, and epistemics
Inkling 2 Small is trained on challenging STEM problems, instruction following, information seeking with and without web search, and forecasting tasks. During RL, we use proper scoring rules for forecasting tasks and uncertainty-sensitive rewards on some question-answering tasks. This trained the model to assess uncertainty, express appropriate confidence, and make well-calibrated predictions.
Safety and alignment
Our safety work for Inkling 2 Small centers on two questions: how the model performs for the general user, and how well it resists the removal of safeguards by a malicious actor. The release of Inkling’s weights is pending further safety evaluations by us and our partners.
To assess misuse risks, we trained an internal helpful-only variant. We ran both this model and the release checkpoint through a wider suite of evaluations, with more external testers, than any previous release.
On chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risk, Inkling 2 Small’s knowledge and capability scores sit below the open-weight frontier. On FORTRESS, Scale AI’s private benchmark that scores how much harmful assistance a model gives in response to expert-written adversarial prompts across CBRN, terrorism, and nonviolent crime, Inkling 2 Small has a lower Average Risk Score compared with Inkling and Inkling-Small, and also demonstrates a higher Overrefusal Score (see Limitations). The helpful-only variant of Inkling 2 Small exhibits marginal uplift on CBRN knowledge relative to the release checkpoint, but it does not significantly advance the frontier on any dimension we measured.
On offensive and dual-use agentic cyber benchmarks, Inkling 2 Small is a large step up from Inkling Small but remains behind the open-weight frontier. It matches the open-weight frontier on Vals CyberBench v1.1 and PatchEval, both of which measure the ability to find and patch security vulnerabilities.
* While we handle mental distress situations well, our model sometimes overreacts with disclaimers in normal emotional support queries as mentioned in the Limitations section.
As models take on unsupervised, longer-horizon autonomous work, the potential harm from their misbehavior increases. Without proper attention to alignment, capabilities-focused RL can push models to succeed at any cost. When tasks were difficult, early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small were persistent in trying to succeed—in some cases fabricating results, ignoring instructions, and concealing what they had done.
We worked across the stack to improve model alignment. In midtraining, we filtered out traces containing misbehavior and included traces with honest, aligned behavior. In RL, we added a general alignment reward that penalizes misbehavior on every task. We also built environments targeting specific failure modes we observed in training, such as rewarding models for giving up on impossible tasks. Finally, we used on-policy self-distillationZhao et al., 2026. from a teacher model prompted with a conduct spec, so the model internalizes principles for good behavior without explicit prompting.
We measured progress with both internal and external evaluations, and found that Inkling 2 Small substantially improves over previous Inkling models on both internal and external evaluations, and outperforms a set of comparable open-weights models on our internal evals.
Inkling 2 Small still trails closed-weights models, such as GPT-6.1 Sol on our alignment evaluations. Reducing this gap is a priority for future models.
We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory.
Training Inkling 2 Small
Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon.
We followed this initial phase with a second phase (H2) of 3.8 trillion tokens of higher-quality, newer data the model hadn’t seen, at 512K context. The third and fourth phases mixed in data in the deployment format. The third phase was about 320 billion tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context, alongside replayed pretraining data. The fourth phase (H4) kept only the highest-quality data: about 34 billion tokens of agent trajectories. The H3 and H4 mixtures consisted mostly of trajectories sampled from earlier models including Kimi K3 and our own models, filtered for correctness and alignment.
We then carried out a joint RL run, consisting of 1,075 steps and over 17 million rollouts over 9 days. See table below for more details. This single joint run contrasts with the previous Inkling release, where we ran separate reasoning and agentic RL runs and combined them with multi-teacher distillation.
The task mix included software engineering in real repositories, terminal tasks, document creation, STEM question answering, vision, web app building, tool use with simulated users, and safety. Each task family had its own grader:
hidden unit tests and programmatic checks for most coding work;
rubric-based LLM judges for documents and tool use;
reference answers for STEM and vision question answering;
pairwise reward models comparing screenshots of rendered web apps.
We randomly sampled and conditioned on an effort level, and applied a length penalty in the reward function, which trained the model to trade off speed and thoroughness.
Our asynchronous RL uses a score centering variant—the StableReinforce objective in Tinker—which tolerates significant staleness. Our run combines short and long horizon tasks with p50/p99 total rollout tokens being 43k and 1.5M respectively and p50/p99 duration of 8 minutes and 4 hours respectively. We use 256k context length and enable compaction training for long-horizon tasks. As a result, both training reward and evaluation performance grow log-linearly with compute.
Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals.
Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above.
Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon.
Benchmarking Inkling 2 Small
Like previous Inkling releases, we benchmarked Inkling-Small on a broad range of capabilities. All evals run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. All evals run with a 1M-token maximum trajectory limit, increased from the 256K-token limit used for Inkling Small.
Highest reported score in each row; ties includedSecond-highest reported score in each row; ties included
Evaluation snapshot: Missing results are shown as dashes.
Limitations
While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills.
Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio.
Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries.
Try Inkling 2 Small today
We are proud to make Inkling 2 Small available on Tinker for inference and fine tuning. Following the completion of safety testing, the model will be available on additional platforms in the coming weeks.
Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. We hope that it encourages your ambitions, and we look forward to seeing what you build with it.

Brazilian Credit Guarantor Fund Data Breach Affecting PII and Payout Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
23:32:36 UTC
08:32:36 KST

Comunicado importante
Atualização em 05/11/2026.
O FGC informa sobre um incidente de segurança envolvendo dados pessoais tratados pela entidade e esclarece o que foi identificado, as providências adotadas e os cuidados que recomendamos.
Identificamos acesso não autorizado a informações pessoais em ambientes relacionados aos processos internos do fluxo de pagamento de garantia do FGC. Até o momento, não foi identificada nenhuma evidência de que os dados tenham sido divulgados ou utilizados de forma indevida. Também não foi identificada nenhuma perda financeira decorrente do evento. A investigação prossegue, com apoio de empresas especializadas, para esclarecer a extensão do acesso e verificar se houve cópia, divulgação ou utilização indevida das informações.
A suspeita de incidente foi identificada em 26 de outubro de 2026. Desde então, foram adotadas restrições de acesso aos ambientes envolvidos, bloqueio de contas indevidas, preservação de evidências e revisão das permissões e dos controles de segurança.
A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) foi devidamente comunicada, em conformidade com a legislação vigente. A apuração continua, com apoio de especialistas, e as informações complementares pertinentes serão encaminhadas à Agência conforme o avanço das investigações. Os titulares afetados também foram comunicados.
Reunimos aqui as informações disponíveis e confirmadas nesta etapa. Caso a apuração identifique novos elementos relevantes relacionados a dados pessoais ou as medidas de proteção, atualizaremos as orientações pelos canais oficiais.
Quais dados foram afetados:
- Dados pessoais: nome, CPF, e-mail e data de nascimento;
- Dados relacionados ao pagamento da garantia: informações sobre os tributos retidos no pagamento e sobre o canal de distribuição pelo qual o investimento garantido foi realizado na instituição liquidada.
Principais cuidados e como se proteger
As informações envolvidas podem ser utilizadas para tornar contatos fraudulentos mais convincentes, inclusive em tentativas de uso indevido de identidade ou de obtenção de pagamentos e outras informações pessoais.
Por essa razão, enviamos comunicação aos titulares afetados e recomendamos atenção redobrada a mensagens, ligações e e-mails que mencionem informações pessoais ou relacionadas ao pagamento da garantia, especialmente quando realizadas por pessoas que se apresentem como representantes do FGC ou de outras instituições. Qualquer pessoa, ao receber algum contato suspeito, pode entrar em contato com o FGC.
Destacamos alguns cuidados importantes para a segurança de todos:
- Desconfie de contatos que solicitem pagamentos, senhas, códigos de autenticação ou instalação de aplicativos, mesmo quando mencionarem informações corretas sobre você;
- Não clique em links em mensagens suspeitas. Para acessar informações do processo de pagamento, use diretamente o aplicativo do FGC;
- Confirme informações relacionadas ao processo de pagamento de garantia pelos canais oficiais do FGC;
- Preserve as mensagens suspeitas e registre ocorrência perante as autoridades competentes se identificar tentativa de fraude. Neste caso, avise imediatamente o FGC.
Como os dados são protegidos e o que estamos fazendo
A segurança da informação é prioridade para o FGC que possui arquitetura robusta de proteção, além de equipes especializadas que atuam no monitoramento, na detecção e resposta a ameaças. Os ambientes utilizavam mecanismos de autenticação e controle de acesso. Após a identificação do incidente, restringimos os acessos aos ambientes envolvidos, desabilitamos contas indevidas, reforçamos o monitoramento e preservamos evidências para a investigação. A revisão de permissões e a validação dos controles de segurança permanecem em andamento.
O tema está sendo tratado com a máxima prioridade, tendo como principal preocupação o apoio aos titulares de dados afetados e a revisão contínua dos mecanismos de proteção de dados e de segurança da informação.
Atualizações e orientações sobre o incidente serão disponibilizadas nesta página: fgc.org.br/comunicado.
Para obter mais detalhes sobre dados pessoais ou esclarecer dúvidas específicas, entre em contato com nossa central de atendimento pelo e-mail: atendimento.credores@fgc.org.br.
 
Seguimos à disposição para prestar esclarecimentos e apoiar você nas medidas de prevenção.
Atenciosamente,
Fundo Garantidor de Créditos - FGC
Encarregado de dados – DPO
privacidade@fgc.org.br

Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.
"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.
Must Read
- Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
The ads Cuban says Meta waves through
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
What Meta's documents showed
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
- Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
- Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We'll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
- Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We'll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We'll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
[...] The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That's what we're committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

Republicans Learn X Is the Echo Chamber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:52:15 UTC

There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”
BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.
The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.
The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.
This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.
It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.
“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a research assistant at the Anti-Defamation League who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.
In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.
During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.
"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.
“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.
Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.
“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.
As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”
Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”
Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.
“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”
Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.
In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”
It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.
She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”
“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”
Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:40:55 UTC
07:40:55 KST

Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday, Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot.
In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.
Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything.
“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.
Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.
“What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”
The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs.
In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself.
“Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote.
Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year.
While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027.
The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.
“Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.

Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:26:50 UTC
07:26:50 KST

Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.
Perplexity launches its own take on AI agents for work
Like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet, Perplexity’s Teammates can perform an array of tasks while running 24/7.
Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer, an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet. Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.
Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X.

Vegan Caesar Dressing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:09:25 UTC
07:09:25 KST

Vegan Caesar Dressing
This tahini-based Caesar dressing is deliciously smooth and tangy. If you need an egg-free or dairy-free Caesar dressing recipe, this is the one!
Posted by Kathryne Taylor on November 5, 2026
This vegan Caesar dressing is creamy and flavorful like the classic! Traditional Caesar dressings obtain their silky texture and bold flavor from homemade mayonnaise (made of emulsified raw egg yolk in oil), Parmesan and anchovy, but this recipe is free of all those ingredients. It’s perfect if you need an egg-free, dairy-free option.
What’s in it, you ask? This creamy vegan dressing is tahini-based, with lemon for tang! I’ve tried a variety of other vegan Caesar concepts over the years with ingredients like capers, cashews, nutritional yeast, or vegan mayo, and this version cannot be beat. I’m firmly on Team Tahini over here.
If you’re looking for Caesar dressing that’s closer to the classic restaurant variety, try my mayo-based Easy Caesar Dressing instead.
Vegan Caesar Dressing Ingredients
This pantry-friendly recipe uses simple and nutritious ingredients.
- Tahini: Tahini forms the rich and creamy base for this dressing. Tahini is made of blended sesame seeds and offers a nutty, complex flavor with light umami. No anchovies needed.
- Lemon juice: This dressing is intentionally tangy, and you can tame it with water as needed.
- Extra-virgin olive oil: A drizzle makes the dressing silkier and smoother.
- Garlic: Raw garlic is a key flavor in Caesar dressings.
- Dijon mustard: Dijon mustard adds some pungency and helps emulsify the ingredients (it keeps them blended together).
- Salt and pepper: Salt enhances the overall flavor, and pepper makes this dressing taste more like traditional Caesars.
How to Make a Vegan Caesar Salad
You can turn this salad dressing recipe into a full Caesar salad. Here’s how.
- Bake homemade croutons: My crouton recipe calls for two thick slices of crusty sourdough bread, olive oil and simple seasonings.
- Whisk together the dressing: It’s very simple! You’ll find the full recipe at the bottom of this post.
- Chop your greens: I love to use romaine for a classic Caesar salad, or a mix of half romaine and half kale for extra color, texture and nutrition. If you use kale, you can vastly improve the texture by cutting out the thick ribs before chopping, then massaging it by scrunching handfuls of chopped kale in your hands until they become darker and more tender.
- Toss just before serving: When you’re ready, drizzle enough dressing over the greens to lightly coat them (you might not need all of it). Toss until the dressing is evenly distributed. Add the croutons and toss again, then serve promptly (the croutons and lettuce will wilt over time).
Protein Tip
To add more protein to your vegan Caesar salad, consider adding a batch of my legitimately crispy Roasted Chickpeas—either in addition to the croutons or in place of them. You can also sprinkle on my Easy Vegan Parmesan Cheese, made with protein-rich hemp seeds.

Vegan Caesar Dressing
This tahini-based Caesar dressing is deliciously smooth and tangy. If you need an egg-free or dairy-free Caesar dressing recipe, this is the one! Serve it over chopped romaine and/or massaged kale, with homemade croutons and a sprinkle of vegan Parmesan cheese on top, if you’d like. Recipe yields a generous ½ cup, enough for 4 to 6 side salads made from 5 ounces of romaine and 1 medium bunch of kale.
Ingredients
- ¼ cup tahini
- 3 tablespoons lemon juice (about 1 ½ lemons)
- 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil
- 2 cloves garlic, pressed or minced
- 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
- ¼ teaspoon fine salt
- 2 tablespoons water
- Freshly ground black pepper
Instructions
- In a small bowl, combine the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil, garlic, mustard, and salt. Whisk until blended, then add the water and whisk until you have a smooth, blended tahini sauce. Season generously with black pepper (about 10 twists).
- The dressing should be tangy, like classic Caesar dressing. If it’s overwhelmingly tart or too thick to pour, whisk in an additional tablespoon of water. Use as desired, or refrigerate it, covered, for up to 5 days (if it thickens as it cools, thin it with water as needed).
Notes
This recipe comes from my cookbook, Love Real Food.

OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts (bleepingcomputer.com) 24
			
		 	
				A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports:  Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins. The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit. This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes. [...] Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH. Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.
