Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:52:36 UTC
03:52:36 KST

The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
Posted on November 5, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 1 Comment
Being the middle child isn’t easy, but the bonds you form with your siblings can be some of the closest and most impactful relationships in your life. Author Daryl Gregory shares memories of his sisters from his childhood, and talks about how their bond played a roll in creating his newest novel, The Porcelain Sisters.
DARYL GREGORY:
Is there something wrong with me that I find two sisters fighting with each other to be hugely entertaining? I was the middle child, the boy sandwiched between two girls—one who was seven years older than me, and the other sixteen months younger. We grew up in a small ranch house in the suburbs of Chicago, and we fought what I assumed was a normal amount.
Ninety percent of the time, it was me versus one of them. With my older sister, this was often when she ordered me to do something, and my go-to response was to slam a door and shout, “You’re not the boss of me!” (She was absolutely the boss of me.)
My younger sister and I were closer in age and so spent more time together, which meant more opportunities to torture each other. I liked to hide in her room and jump-scare her. She’s the finest screamer in the family, and terrifying her is extremely satisfying. She knew how to hit back, though. One time she kidnapped my prized possession, a G.I. Joe with lifelike hair and Kung Fu grip, and he reappeared days later with a bald spot, as if his forced marriage to Barbie had driven him into middle age. I still have him—and the damage is outrageous.
So it was a delight—a delight, I tell you—when my sisters fought with each other, and I got sit on the sidelines munching my proverbial popcorn.
But here’s the thing I found amazing—their fights were so short. They’d pivot from shouting at each other to calmly hanging out in their shared bedroom. They didn’t hold grudges. (I, however, was a champion pouter.) Even now, if they have an argument, they repair the damage quickly. I love my sisters, and they’ve assured me that they love me back, but they have a bond with each other that I find mysterious and enviable.
So perhaps it’s not a surprise that sisters turn up a lot in my books. Ruth and Isabel, the two main characters in my new novella, The Porcelain Sisters, are not exactly like my siblings—for one thing, neither of mine is a haunted doll—but let’s just say there are… similarities.
Ruth (the flesh-and-blood sister) and Isabel (the porcelain one) first appeared as teenagers in my YA Lovecraftian horror novel, Harrison Squared. They were my favorite characters to write dialog for, because they operated almost like a vaudeville ventriloquist act—Ruth was shy and soft-spoken, while Isabel spoke the truth and cut everyone down to size.
But in that book I never explained why Isabel could talk, or how they were sisters, or where Isabel came from. That was for a good reason: I didn’t know. I wrote this book to find out—and to get the chance to hang out with them some more.
Ruth, now in her twenties, is trying to make rent while taking college classes, but feeling adrift. She seems to have some latent magical ability, but doesn’t know what her purpose in life is beyond taking care of her sister. She’s never even had a long-term romantic relationship because Isabel deliberately freaks out anybody she brings home.
Isabel’s anger issues stem, of course, from being trapped in a porcelain body. She can’t grow up and may never live on her own. When her body’s accidentally damaged during a fight with Ruth—a seaside cliff is involved—a mundane toy repair shop won’t cut it. They have to go on the road to find the Dollmaker, the French witch who made her.
As I wrote that last sentence I realized the sisters are literally repairing each other. I wish I’d thought of that in time to put it on the back cover copy.
The girls head to Marseille, where they face off with an unkillable assassin with the resilience of a ragdoll, a pair of demons (one a chain-smoking crow, the other a black cat) and their human familiars, as well as a small army of haunted dolls. Oh, and the Dollmaker turns out to be the head of Le Clan des Sorciéres, a kind of witch mafia. I know, it’s a lot.
At the root of the mystery is why their mother, an enforcer for Le Clan called Godless Annie, abandoned them. What the sisters discover about themselves suggests there may be a way for them to live apart—but do they want to?
Another thing occurred to me as I’m typing this: is that ending about my current relationship with my sisters? Since our mom passed we don’t see each other like we used to. We live on opposite sides of the country, and our lives are busy. Did I write this book because I miss them?
I suppose I could talk to a therapist about this. Or write another book about sisters. Or—and hear me out—I could go on the road with the Gregory girls, solving mysteries and fighting the occasional demon.
The Porcelain Sisters: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s

US government warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:48:34 UTC
03:48:34 KST

The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.
“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.
The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.
Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.
The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.
CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

Republicans learn X is the echo chamber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:27:34 UTC
03:27:34 KST

There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”
BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.
The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.
The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.
This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.
It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.
“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a research assistant at the Anti-Defamation League who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.
In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.
During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.
"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.
“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.
Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.
“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.
As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”
Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”
Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.
“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”
Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.
In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”
It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.
She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”
“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”
Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:24:28 UTC
03:24:28 KST

- Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way.
- Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated.
- We’ve open sourced everything, including the protocol, server, client through Meta’s Time library on GitHub.
- We’re also encouraging everyone, particularly those who maintain an NTP client on Android or iOS, to join us in enabling NTS support.
We’ve previously written about building a more accurate time service at Meta scale – migrating from ntpd to chrony, going from 10 milliseconds to 100 microseconds, and opening time.meta.com to everyone.
That work made time precise. This work makes it verifiable.
Why NTS?
NTP has been unauthenticated since 1985, like a lot of the internet’s foundational protocols. But it is also the one every certificate, token, and signature is checked against. The client sends 48 bytes, something sends 48 bytes back, and the client believes it. There is no signature and no identity.
It is not alone in that. Plenty of the internet’s foundational protocols were designed for a network where nobody was assumed to be hostile, and the industry has been retrofitting them ever since. What makes time different is that it is not just another protocol to secure. It is the input every other security decision is measured against.
For most of NTP’s life that did not matter much, because a clock being a few seconds off was an operational annoyance. Today it is load-bearing:
- Certificate validation: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the local clock. Wrong clock, wrong answer.
- Token and credential expiry: “Valid for 15 minutes” is a claim about a clock.
- Replay windows: Rejecting a request older than N seconds requires knowing what time it is.
- Log correlation and ordering: Two hosts that disagree produce a timeline that never happened.
And the check itself is circular. You can’t do X.509 notBefore/notAfter validation without knowing the current time. Effectively you’d have to disable cert time validation, or implement one of the suggested work-arounds.
There are two common workarounds. Both are bad. You can skip validation until the clock is set, which leaves a device unprotected exactly when it is most exposed. Or you can build in-slack: A certificate issued at 12:00:00 is rejected by a client whose clock reads 11:59:30, so issuers backdate notBefore by a few minutes and validators quietly widen the window at their end. Both sides are guessing at how wrong the other one is.
That was survivable when a certificate lasted 398 days. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 changed that. The cap on newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped to 200 days in March 2026, falls to 100 days in March 2027, and reaches 47 days in March 2029 — with domain validation reuse dropping to 10 days at the same point.
At 47 days, manual certificate management stops being viable at any scale. Renewal moves to roughly monthly, and it happens unattended — usually over ACME. An automated renewal loop on a host with a skewed clock does not raise a ticket. It reissues, or it fails, on a schedule nobody is watching.
How NTS Works
NTS works in phases, and separating them is what makes it deployable.
Phase 1 – Key Establishment (NTS-KE): TLS 1.3 over TCP/4460, negotiated with ALPN ntske/1. The client and server agree on an AEAD algorithm, then derive two directional session keys (C2S and S2C) straight from the TLS session using the RFC 5705 exporter. The server issues eight cookies, tells the client which NTP server to actually use via a server negotiation record, and closes the connection. This happens once, not per packet.
We negotiate three AEADs: AES-SIV-CMAC-256 (ID 15), which RFC 8915 makes mandatory to implement and is what an unknown client is most likely to ask for; AES-SIV-CMAC-512 (17); and AES-128-GCM-SIV (30). Client preference wins.
Phase 2 – Authenticated NTP: Standard NTPv4 over UDP/123 to the advertised server, with NTS extension fields. A request carries a unique identifier, a cookie, and an authenticator; the authenticator covers everything before it, but encrypts nothing. The server opens the cookie to recover the session keys, verifies that authenticator, and replies with the unique identifier echoed back plus an authenticator of its own – and that one does carry a payload: the fresh cookies, encrypted inside it.
A forged packet fails verification and is dropped. We do not send an NTS NAK, so a failure is indistinguishable from packet loss and cannot be used to push a client into a fresh key exchange. A replayed response carries the wrong unique identifier and matches no outstanding request. Because the replacement cookies ride inside the response authenticator rather than in the clear, an observer sees a different opaque blob every exchange and cannot follow a client between networks. Spending each cookie once is the client’s side of that bargain – the server is stateless and does not track them.
Cookies Without State
A cookie is a server state handed to the client for safekeeping. It holds the session keys, sealed with AES-SIV so only the server can open it. The obvious implementation is a key ring replicated to every server, which turns time service into a distributed state problem.
We do not replicate keys. Each server derives the sealing key from a shared master secret and the current day:
Since the Unix epoch, day is measured as whole 24-hour periods,  not a calendar day. So there is no timezone and no DST, and every host computes the same integer for the same instant. That integer is the cookie’s key ID and travels in the clear. A server that has been handed a cookie it has never seen or sealed by a host it has never talked to, re-derives the key and opens it. We accept two days back and one forward to cover skew around a rotation boundary.
The result is no key ring, no replication, no session table, no shared state to fall out of sync, and nothing for an attacker to exhaust. It is also what makes the split above work – the KE server and the NTP servers it hands you off to are different machines in different places, and they never exchange anything. Adding a server is adding a server.
The plain NTP path is untouched. The responder parses extension fields only when they are present, so unauthenticated clients hit the same code as before at the same cost.
Using NTS
One line of chrony config:
nts.meta.com terminates key exchange only. During the handshake it advertises an NTP responder in a server negotiation record, so the client is steered to time.meta.com and sends its authenticated NTP there. The host you configure is not the host you end up talking to.
That indirection is why we use pool rather than server. A single server line gives you one association and one responder, which is a single point of failure – and NTP is a protocol that wants several sources so it can outvote a bad one. pool asks for maxsources independent associations. Each runs its own key exchange over its own TLS session, so each ends up with a distinct pair of session keys:
Five rows, five independent authenticated sources, from one line of config and one KE endpoint.
Reading across: Type 30 is the negotiated AEAD, AES-128-GCM-SIV, with KLen 128 bits of session key — chrony lists it first and client preference wins. CLen 68 is the cookie: 36 bytes of envelope around the two 16-byte keys inside. Cook 8 is cookies in hand and NAK 0 means none has been rejected.
The more interesting half is not in the table. Each row’s session keys came out of its own TLS handshake and work only for that association. The key that seals them into a cookie is the shared one – the epoch day number from the derivation above, identical on every responder we run, stamped inside each cookie and never visible to the client. That split is what lets a single key exchange hand a client five different responders that have never spoken to each other.
When a pool member completes key exchange and moves to its negotiated responder, the freed KE address is handed to the next unresolved member, repeating until maxsources responders have answered. Five sources come up in about 20 minutes as each member completes its own key exchange in turn.
NTS Protects Against Attacks
Unlike NTP, NTS stops a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack from forging the answer. A classic MITM attack doesn’t need to break any cryptography, it just has to answer a client before a real server does. If an attacker rolls the clock backward they can make expired certificates validate again or revoked tokens work again. Any control that relies on something having expired is reset. If they roll the clock forward everything expires at once. This is the more difficult direction to address because beyond a certain point the failure stops being recoverable.
Let’s look at an example of what happens to a device that gets convinced it is the year 2037. NTP counts seconds in a 32-bit field that wraps in February 2036, and a client stranded on the far side of that boundary computes its correction into the wrong era – so the mechanism that exists to fix a wrong clock now moves it further away. Meanwhile every certificate the device holds is long expired, so TLS fails, therefore it cannot reach anything that might help, including its own update service. The patch that would fix it cannot be delivered, because delivering it needs the clock that is broken.
The device is not damaged. Every component works exactly as designed. It is simply holding a number that puts it outside the reach of the network. And no amount of waiting or rebooting fixes it. Recovery means a factory reset, or a trip to a service center. Multiply that by a fleet and the cost of a wrong integer becomes a logistics problem.
Now, consider a clock forward attack on a host that issues credentials. Short-lived credentials are considered safe because they expire quickly, which means short lifetime is doing the job revocation would otherwise do. That property is entirely a function of the issuing host’s clock. An issuer convinced it is next year signs credentials that outlive the window you designed for.
What NTS Does Not Fix
Delay attacks. RFC 8915 is explicit. An attacker who holds your packets shifts your clock by up to half the delay introduced, and no cryptography in the protocol detects it, because every byte is genuine. Authentication tells you who wrote a packet, not how long it spent in flight. Mitigations are the usual ones – multiple independent sources, sanity limits, bounded steps.
So the claim is narrow: An on-path attacker can still delay your packets and can still drop them. What they can no longer do is lie about the contents.
Bootstrapping. NTS-KE runs over TLS and TLS wants a working clock, which is the same circular problem as above. A device with a dead RTC still has to get roughly correct before its first handshake.
Wrong servers. NTS authenticates the path, not the answer. A server that is correctly configured, correctly authenticated, and simply wrong will hand you the wrong time with a perfect signature on it. Quorum, sanity checks, and monitoring are still required.
Monotonicity. Authenticated time is still wall-clock time, and wall clocks move backward — at a leap second, or whenever a correction lands. Cloudflare’s authoritative DNS hit this at the end of 2016: a resolver round-trip measured across the leap second came out negative, propagated into upstream selection, and panicked Go’s rand.Int63n(). Nothing was forged and nothing was misdelivered. If your code measures elapsed time, use a monotonic clock.
Adoption
RFC 8915, Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol, was published on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard in September 2020. Cloudflare had launched time.cloudflare.com with NTS 15 months earlier, in June 2019, against the then-current draft, and showed it works at scale.
Server-side, the public NTS list today runs to a few dozen entries, mostly national metrology institutes and internet infrastructure operators such as PTB, Netnod, and time.nl. We are adding one more.
The bigger gap is on the client. NTS support exists where you would expect it in the server world – chrony and ntpsec implement it. It is absent entirely from the stock time client on the platforms that account for most of the endpoints on the internet.
Android’s platform time sync is plain SNTP over UDP/123 – a fixed 48-byte packet with no extension-field handling, alongside NITZ and GNSS – so there is no NTS path in it. Apple devices sync through timed against time.apple.com, where we are not aware of any NTS support either.
Those two stacks set the clock on billions of phones, watches and headsets, and every one of them is trusting an unauthenticated UDP packet. A device vendor can ship a separate NTS-capable client today — chrony runs perfectly well on Android – but that is a workaround for something the platform should do itself.
The protocol is finished, the servers are appearing, the client implementations exist.
What is missing is mobile.
Join Us in Enabling NTS
nts.meta.com is live and free. The code is in github.com/facebook/time.
If you run a public time service, turn NTS on. If you maintain an NTP client, implement RFC 8915. If you own the time stack in a mobile OS, this is the gap – Android and iOS are where most of the world’s clocks get set, and both of them are still doing it over an unauthenticated packet.
We have spent years making time more precise. Precision without authenticity only gets you a very accurate number from an unknown source. Now it can be both.

OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:02:27 UTC
03:02:27 KST

OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.
In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.”
“We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said.
He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.
“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”
By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point.
Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue.
“And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with.
Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.
“A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’” Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.”

The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.
Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.
Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.
One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.
Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.
His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.
Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”
After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.
The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)
What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.
By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”
Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”
Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.
That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.
It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.
Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.
He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.
Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.
The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.
Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.
Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”
In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”
Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.
“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”
He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are outraising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.
That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.
Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”
For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.
Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)
Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.
Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight and is a principal at Brightmind.
CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.
Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.
For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”
Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

Anthropic announced Thursday that Claude is getting a new tool called “Personal Finance,” designed to help users keep track of their money. With it, users can connect their bank and credit card accounts through Plaid and ask Claude questions about their finances. Anthropic says access is read-only, meaning Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest users’ money.
By letting Claude connect directly to bank and credit card accounts, Anthropic is positioning its chatbot as a financial companion that can help people understand their spending and make sense of their money, rather than simply offering them generic advice.
With the launch, Claude is playing catch-up to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which introduced similar personal finance tools in May that also let users connect their financial accounts and ask questions about everything from spending patterns to long-term financial planning.
“Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that’s new to you,” Anthropic wrote in a blog post. “Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.”
For instance, at the end of the month, a user could ask Claude, “Where did my money go this month?” The chatbot will then add up spending across the connected accounts and sort it by category, such as rent and utilities, food and drink, and shopping. Users can choose to go deeper by following up with questions like, “Is that more than usual?” or “Anything else I’m missing?”
Anthropic says the tool goes beyond basic spending summaries by analyzing transactions across connected accounts to flag potential issues, such as duplicate charges, unexpected fees, and steadily increasing bills. Users can also ask broader questions about their finances, such as whether they’re spending more than they earn. The tool can also explain financial concepts like APR (annual percentage rate), while providing calculations that show users how much they’ve paid in interest over the past year.
Of course, some people will have reservations about connecting their financial accounts to an AI chatbot. Anthropic says Claude’s access is limited to each connected bank’s name, account name and type, the last four digits of the account number, balances, credit limits, and up to two years of transaction history.
Additionally, the company notes that when users chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train its models.
Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week to users on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the U.S.
The launch of the new tool comes as Anthropic has been expanding Claude into new verticals. For instance, Anthropic launched Claude for Legal and Claude for Financial Services earlier this year.

Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.
Privately, CEOs have discussed significant compute capacity constraints for their companies after Tuesday’s results, particularly OpenAI, per The Wall Street Journal. Meta’s platforms president, Dina Powell McCormick, says many are considering moving data center construction abroad. AI executives are reportedly privately nervous about the results but may also be able to blame them for not delivering as much revenue to investors. Many of the incoming leaders have promised to drag CEOs to testify. On X, a popular post by former X product lead Nikita Bier warned that “This is going to be like the Nuremberg Trials but for AI researchers.” (On Tuesday night, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did post about how “people should always be in control of the future,” but he spent other parts of the evening talking about RAM.)
Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”
The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.
“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.
In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.
“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.
“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.
“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.
Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”
OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.
“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.
“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.
But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”
Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.
There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).
President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.
“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.

Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.
Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.
Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.
Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.
If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.
Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:
“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

My gym forced a social media down my throat. So I reverse-engineered its app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:30:17 UTC
02:30:17 KST

My gym forced a social media down my throat. I reverse-engineered its app.
I recently joined a new gym. It’s a pretty good gym, with nice equipment, nice management, nice branding.
And an app.
Now, it’s not some random shitty vibe-coded app. It’s actually pretty good as a product. It has pretty slick UI/UX and a well-thought-out, consistent design language. I found only one bug in it.
For me, though, the only use case is to show a QR code at the turnstile for checking in and out.
However, there is a problem. The home screen of the app is a social feed. Once you check out, it prompts you to post a story of your session. The home feed is full of people’s gym selfies. Every time I open the app, I’m forced to see something that essentially looks like Tinder.
Now, my friend thinks this is a genius business idea. According to her, people who work out really want to flaunt their bodies, but posting that on normal social media is frowned upon. So this gym company really found a good product-market fit.
I think she’s right.
However, I’m super aggressive about social media and feeds I don’t control. Any app that shows me a feed I can’t turn off, sort, or filter—I take that as psychological warfare against me.
I haven’t used social media in more than 12 years. I’m super adamant about blocking ads, blocking YouTube comments, Shorts, and suggested videos, and sanitizing YouTube titles and thumbnails. For things I must use, like LinkedIn1, I use browser extensions to block the news feed completely.
So I took it personally.
I wanted to see if I could extract the QR-code logic without all the extra bloat of the app.
So I started digging. I quickly found out that the code changes every 15 seconds. Screenshots are also blocked on that screen, consistent with Android’s FLAG_SECURE. I wondered if it was some kind of TOTP. Was the generation happening server-side?
I did the simplest thing: turned off Wi-Fi. The app immediately told me the codes would remain valid for N days without reconnecting2.
Okay, so it could generate them locally.
I used GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. In my sessions, GLM was burning something like 10–20 times as much in token cost without making that much progress. DeepSeek seemed to move much faster.
To be clear, I’m leaving out some details to keep the gym and myself anonymous. I don’t want to lose my gym subscription. I actually like that gym.
The app was written in Flutter, with most of the logic compiled into Dart native code. We used blutter to inspect that, jadx for the Android-side code, and Android’s SDK tools to inspect the package. Later, we used OpenSSL and WebCrypto to check the encryption, and zbar to decode the QR codes independently.
I was prompting DeepSeek here and there, mostly from intuition, because I’d never done this before. Sometimes it seemed to get lost in a direction where I felt the implementation must be simpler than that. Just telling it my guesses, or saying that I thought there must be a simpler way, helped steer it in the right direction.
We quickly understood that the QR code was a URL containing four things: an encoded account handle, an encrypted expiry timestamp, a random nonce, and a checksum.
The expiry was encrypted using AES-128-CTR. A separate secret was used to calculate the checksum. So we needed those two secrets for my account.
My first idea was to let DeepSeek drive an Android emulator, sign in, and extract the keys. But I quickly realized that my ten-year-old laptop, borrowed from a friend, wasn’t going to handle Android software emulation at any reasonable speed.
DeepSeek suggested a rooted phone. That’s when I remembered I had a functional rooted Android phone lying around.
I booted it, connected over wireless ADB, and let DeepSeek investigate. It turned out that the app logged the request and response payloads for the calls we cared about. The key material was sitting in a plain text log file on the phone.
Half of this project was ripgrep.
With the keys extracted, we built a simple SvelteKit web app to generate the QR codes.
There were a few wrong assumptions along the way. The expiry timestamp needed to be in milliseconds, not seconds. The encoding was base64url, not standard base64, and it kept the padding.
We also had an incorrect AES implementation that passed its own round-trip tests. It encrypted something, decrypted it, and got the original input back. But both directions shared the same mistakes, so that didn’t prove it was AES.
Comparing against WebCrypto exposed the discrepancy. OpenSSL and known test vectors confirmed it. The browser app uses WebCrypto.
We then checked against actual output from the original app. Given the same inputs, our implementation produced a byte-identical URL. We also decoded the QR image independently to check that it contained the right URL.
At that point, we had a working prototype. The web app could generate the codes locally from the extracted keys. This didn’t solve standalone login or remove the need to obtain fresh keys when they rotated, but it was enough to try it at the gym.
The next day, I headed there, very proudly showing my friend what I’d built, but still a bit uncertain whether it would work at the gate.
And voilà, it did!
Check-in and check-out.
No more being forced to get my attention hijacked by dark-patterned, manipulative social media just to enter an establishment to lift some metals.
Footnotes
- For the longest time, my LinkedIn bio was “I HATE LINKEDIN.” Someone told me LinkedIn combines the worst of the corporate world with the worst of social media, and I think that only half describes how bad it really is. But alas, I’m in the job market right now, and I need a LinkedIn profile for applications.↩
- I’m not revealing the exact number of days to help keep the app anonymous.↩

Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:17:42 UTC
02:17:42 KST

4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions
Quickstart • Documentation • Blog • Discord • X
Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.
- 72 KB per Actor: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands.
- 4.99 ms p99 cold starts: No image pull and no VM boot.
- Built for scale: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors.
- Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.
- SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.
- Durable & multiplayer AI agents: memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client
- Workflows: multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over
- AI-generated apps: run the apps and Actors your agent generates
- Collaborative editing: one Actor per document, synced to every editor
A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use Pi Durable.
// server.ts
import { actor, setup } from "rivetkit";
import { db } from "rivetkit/db";
import { streamText } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
// One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"])
export const agent = actor({
  // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts
  db: db({
    onMigrate: async (db) => {
      await db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)");
    },
  }),
  // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip
  createVars: () => ({ online: new Map<string, string>() }),
  // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them
  onDisconnect: (c, conn) => {
    c.vars.online.delete(conn.id);
    c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
  },
  actions: {
    join: (c, user: string) => {
      c.vars.online.set(c.conn.id, user);
      c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
    },
    sendMessage: async (c, text: string) => {
      // Save the message
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "user", text);
      const messages = await c.db.execute("SELECT role, content FROM messages");
      // Stream tokens to every connected client
      const response = streamText({ model: openai("gpt-5"), messages });
      for await (const delta of response.textStream) {
        c.broadcast("token", delta);
      }
      // Save the response
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "assistant", await response.text);
    },
  },
});
export const registry = setup({ use: { agent } });// client.ts (frontend or backend)
import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client";
import type { registry } from "./server";
const client = createClient<typeof registry>();
// Open a WebSocket connection to the agent
const agent = client.agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]).connect();
// Listen for realtime events
agent.on("online", users => console.log("online:", users));
agent.on("token", delta => process.stdout.write(delta));
// Call actions on the Actor
await agent.join("nathan");
await agent.sendMessage("how many r's in strawberry?");
Each Actor gives the agent a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and hibernation when idle.
Most of an agent's time is spent waiting on inference. When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits mostly idle with low CPU usage.
Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called "separating the head from the hands." The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the blast radius and trust boundary of the code it runs. Read more about running the harness outside of the sandbox.
Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:
- Agents with tools: Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed.
- Agents with a lightweight sandbox: agentOS provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode.
- Agents with a full sandbox: Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a bash tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the sandbox coding agent example.
Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:
Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.
Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.
- Actors: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in.
- Agents: Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts.
- Workflows: Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over.
- agentOS: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits.
- Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated.
Benchmark details & methodology
- Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark, run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them.
- Sandbox numbers are for E2B: 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from E2B's billing documentation as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark.
- Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices.
- Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking.
- Fault tolerance: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact.
- HTTP & WebSocket networking: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it.
- End-to-end type safety: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend.
- Cron & scheduling: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself.
- Actor-to-Actor calls: Actors call each other by key across the cluster.
- Scoped JWTs: Give each client a JWT scoped to the Actors it may reach.
- OpenTelemetry: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format.
Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production. Talk to an engineer →
Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun with no custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.
Deploy nodes on: Docker Compose • Kubernetes • VM & bare metal • Hetzner • AWS ECS • Railway • Render
Runtimes: Node.js • Bun • Rust
Tools: Vitest • OpenTelemetry • Pino • AI SDK • OpenAPI • AsyncAPI
Does Rivet have BYOC?
Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the BYOC docs.
Does Rivet have a cloud?
Yes. Rivet Cloud runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as nodes on Rivet Cloud, or you can bring your own nodes.
Can I self-host Rivet?
Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the self-hosting docs. The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment, contact us.
Do I still need Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS?
No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, or Hetzner Object Storage. A local filesystem backend is available for trying Rivet on one machine.
Is Rivet open-source?
Yes. Rivet is open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. You're looking at it.
Are Rivet Actors only for agents?
No. Rivet is a general actor platform at its core, with nothing specific to agents. For agents, you can use the optional agent library, which runs Pi Durable on Rivet Actors, or write your own agent from scratch.
How does Rivet compare to sandboxes?
A sandbox boots a VM or container per agent, which is slow to start and sits mostly idle. A Rivet Actor runs inside a shared node process: 72 KB and 4.99 ms p99 to start, versus 512 MiB and 1.70 s for a sandbox, and it hibernates when idle. To run untrusted code your agent writes, use agentOS.
How does Rivet compare to Cloudflare Durable Objects?
Rivet is often used as an open-source alternative to Cloudflare Durable Objects that is easy to self-host and scales. It also fixes many of the constraints of Durable Objects: no 128 MB memory cap, bottomless storage instead of a 10 GB SQLite limit, Actors are not randomly evicted, and you control the runtime because Actors run on vanilla Node.js or Bun instead of a custom runtime. Rivet also adds built-in connection handling, event broadcasting, durable scheduling and cron, full Vitest support, lifecycle hooks for draining, and control over Actor upgrades. See the Cloudflare Durable Objects comparison.
Does Rivet use a custom V8 runtime?
No. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.
Is Rivet like Erlang, Akka, or Orleans?
Rivet implements the virtual actor pattern, which is closest to Orleans, but focuses on what modern workloads need: SQLite persistence instead of simple JSON stores and support for modern runtimes. Erlang and Akka do not provide virtual actors out of the box, though ecosystem packages exist that offer functionality comparable to Rivet Actors.
Does Rivet require microVMs, gVisor, or nested virtualization?
No. Rivet only needs a standard process that connects to the control plane over WebSocket. That process can be Node.js, Bun, Rust, or anything else.
