Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:17:42 UTC
02:17:42 KST

4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions
Quickstart • Documentation • Blog • Discord • X
Rivet Actors are long-lived processes with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets, and scheduling. You can create one for each agent, user, session, or tenant.
- 72 KB per Actor: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands.
- 4.99 ms p99 cold starts: No image pull and no VM boot.
- Built for scale: All data lives in S3, so a cluster scales to billions of Actors.
- Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.
- SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage.
- Durable & multiplayer AI agents: memory that survives restarts, shared live with every client
- Workflows: multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over
- AI-generated apps: run the apps and Actors your agent generates
- Collaborative editing: one Actor per document, synced to every editor
A minimal agent written from scratch. For a ready-made agent, use Pi Durable.
// server.ts
import { actor, setup } from "rivetkit";
import { db } from "rivetkit/db";
import { streamText } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
// One Actor per agent, created on first use: agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"])
export const agent = actor({
  // 1. SQLite: every agent has its own database, so history survives restarts
  db: db({
    onMigrate: async (db) => {
      await db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)");
    },
  }),
  // 2. In-memory state: plain variables that live with the Actor, with no database round trip
  createVars: () => ({ online: new Map<string, string>() }),
  // 3. WebSockets: each client holds a live connection, and the Actor pushes to all of them
  onDisconnect: (c, conn) => {
    c.vars.online.delete(conn.id);
    c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
  },
  actions: {
    join: (c, user: string) => {
      c.vars.online.set(c.conn.id, user);
      c.broadcast("online", [...c.vars.online.values()]);
    },
    sendMessage: async (c, text: string) => {
      // Save the message
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "user", text);
      const messages = await c.db.execute("SELECT role, content FROM messages");
      // Stream tokens to every connected client
      const response = streamText({ model: openai("gpt-5"), messages });
      for await (const delta of response.textStream) {
        c.broadcast("token", delta);
      }
      // Save the response
      await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "assistant", await response.text);
    },
  },
});
export const registry = setup({ use: { agent } });// client.ts (frontend or backend)
import { createClient } from "rivetkit/client";
import type { registry } from "./server";
const client = createClient<typeof registry>();
// Open a WebSocket connection to the agent
const agent = client.agent.getOrCreate(["agent-123"]).connect();
// Listen for realtime events
agent.on("online", users => console.log("online:", users));
agent.on("token", delta => process.stdout.write(delta));
// Call actions on the Actor
await agent.join("nathan");
await agent.sendMessage("how many r's in strawberry?");
Each Actor gives the agent a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage for session transcripts and agent artifacts, and hibernation when idle.
Most of an agent's time is spent waiting on inference. When the agent loop runs inside a sandbox, you pay for a whole VM that sits mostly idle with low CPU usage.
Rivet Actors run the agent loop outside of the sandbox instead, often called "separating the head from the hands." The agent's state, memory, and context live in the Actor, and it reaches the sandbox through tools only when it needs to run code. This uses a fraction of the memory and limits the blast radius and trust boundary of the code it runs. Read more about running the harness outside of the sandbox.
Often not. An agent needs a sandbox only to run code it writes. Developers on Rivet use three patterns:
- Agents with tools: Many agents only need tool calls, MCP, and APIs, such as customer support or personal agents. No sandbox needed.
- Agents with a lightweight sandbox: agentOS provides Linux-compatible sandboxing for JS and Python using V8 and WebAssembly, with full POSIX filesystems, networking stacks, and process trees. It covers most workloads, like data analysis, file processing, evals, and code mode.
- Agents with a full sandbox: Keep your existing sandbox provider and expose its shell and filesystem to the agent as tools, such as a bash tool that runs commands in the sandbox. The Actor reattaches to it across sleeps and restarts. See the sandbox coding agent example.
Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:
Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.
Rivet ships libraries built on top of Actors for common use cases.
- Actors: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in.
- Agents: Durable agents built on Actors, with memory that survives restarts.
- Workflows: Multi-step operations built on Actors that replay instead of starting over.
- agentOS: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits.
- Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated.
Benchmark details & methodology
- Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark, run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them.
- Sandbox numbers are for E2B: 512 MiB is its default memory allocation from E2B's billing documentation as of November 4, 2026, and 1.70 s is the p99 cold start from ComputeSDK's October 30, 2026 sandbox benchmark.
- Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices.
- Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking.
- Fault tolerance: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact.
- HTTP & WebSocket networking: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it.
- End-to-end type safety: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend.
- Cron & scheduling: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself.
- Actor-to-Actor calls: Actors call each other by key across the cluster.
- Scoped JWTs: Give each client a JWT scoped to the Actors it may reach.
- OpenTelemetry: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format.

The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:13:42 UTC
02:13:42 KST

It’s the year 2026 and the Federal Aviation Administration is still running critical pieces of American airspace on 3.5-inch magnetic floppy disks.
The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wants credit for dragging America’s air traffic control out of the 1980s, but retiring 3.5-inch floppies won’t fix a broken system running on overworked controllers and private-sector hype.
But those technology artifacts could be headed for the dustbin after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced an effort to ditch floppy disks in favor of a new digital system.
Duffy announced Thursday that the FAA is rolling out the Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) to replace four legacy setups across more than 400 air traffic control facilities. E-IDS aggregates real-time weather alerts, equipment outages, restricted airspace changes, and pilot reports onto a modern digital dashboard, replacing manual workflows and archaic physical storage media.
Upgrades have already kicked off at five sites — including control hubs in Atlantic City, Nashville, Rochester, Atlanta, and Salt Lake City — with a targeted rollout across 435 facilities by the end of 2028.
“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Duffy said in a release.
Duffy, a former reality TV star and Fox Business host, has been using floppy disks as a scapegoat for the air travel disruptions that have plagued the country for years now. He waves them around during speeches or TV interviews, while highlighting that the FAA still uses “copper wires and floppy disks” as a symbol of government obsolescence.
Indeed, our air traffic control system is deeply out of date, especially when held up alongside the more modern approaches of other nations. A Government Accountability Office report from September 2024 found that 90 percent of the nation’s critical air traffic control infrastructure was due or past due for a “technology refresh.” Nearly half of the 138 systems surveyed were “considered unsustainable” or “potentially unsustainable” due to shortfalls in funding, insufficient maintenance expertise, or even a lack of spare parts.
But E-IDS is not an overnight breakthrough cooked up in a single executive sprint; it’s an existing FAA contract that has spent years working through procurement, safety validation, testing, and vendor timelines. The initial contract for E-IDS was awarded to Leidos, a defense contractor headquartered in Reston, Virginia, by the FAA back in August 2020, during the first Trump administration.
The scope of the problem was understood, even back then. But since then, it has gotten much worse. The FAA has faced backlash in recent years over ground stops, close calls on runways (including one involving President Donald Trump), chronic burnout among air traffic controllers, and high-profile software meltdowns, like the 2023 NOTAM outage. Duffy is clearly trying the frame the system’s problems around relics like the floppy disk, as if obsolete tech is the only reason for the disruptions.
But as we’ve noted before, it’s a much bigger problem than just the systems themselves. Replacing an information system with digital panels is relatively low-hanging fruit compared to the systemic crises plaguing American aviation, such as a crippling deficit of thousands of certified professional controllers. Duffy has been lobbying Congress for an additional $30 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion “down payment” he got in 2025, for his ATC modernization plan.
Under Duffy, the USDOT has made a big deal about recruiting gamers, specifically, to take on these roles. And the administration is also relying on its tech oligarch allies, including Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, to help them clean up the mess — even if they happen to make it worse in the process.

Food delivery startup Wonder files for IPO as it explores its next big bite
Unknown

2026-11-05

02:11:48 KST

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.
Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.
Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.
Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.
Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.
Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.
Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

Nasdaq plummets 4% into correction territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:11:15 UTC
02:11:15 KST

Stocks plummeted on Thursday, erasing the sharp gains from the rally seen in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, as investors accelerated their move away from technology stocks on fears of a data-center buildout slowdown.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 5.52% to close at 24,315.00. The tech-heavy index slid into correction territory, falling more than 10% below a record set last month. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to end at 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and settled at 51,523.06.
The Dow more than wiped out its advance from Wednesday's massive postelection rally. All three major averages posted their worst day since April 2025.
The small-cap Russell 2000 index decreased 4.45% and also entered a correction.
Stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade, particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers, slid for a second day. Investors fear that a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as well as victories in key gubernatorial races could decelerate the data center buildout.
For instance, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — who caucuses with Democrats — has called for a national data center moratorium. In a post on X Wednesday evening, Sanders wrote that "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia respectively fell 10% and 9% Thursday, while software stock Oracle moved lower by almost 7%. Another chip stock, Qualcomm, reported earnings that beat estimates, but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down more than 12% for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
Shares of neocloud companies also retreated, with CoreWeave losing almost 10%. Nebius and Iren slid about 15% and almost 17%, amid worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states.
Investors are "stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we've had going for us for the last, call it, three years," said Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion. "It's about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level."
Thursday's selling pressure was so intense that it spread to other parts of the market. Shares of industrial giant Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial stock JPMorgan fell 4%. Aerospace name Boeing and athletic apparel giant Nike pulled back 2%.
"Unlike yesterday, you're just seeing that the sell-off in tech, the size of it, is now feeding itself into the broader market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Wealth. "The rubber band is becoming increasingly stretched."
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025 after a decisive midterm win for Democrats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also popped more than 1% each. Areas related to AI were under pressure, however, while economically-sensitive stocks rose.

OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:10:19 UTC
02:10:19 KST

OpenAI is launching GPT-6 Cyber, the latest version of its cybersecurity AI model, which it says is better at finding vulnerabilities and less likely to go rogue and hack other platforms in the process. OpenAI says that during testing, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds less than 1 percent of the time, down from around 5 percent with GPT-5.6 Cyber.
OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
Classified as ‘Critical,’ GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra on cyber-related benchmarks.
The evaluation, called ExploitGym HoneyPot, is modeled after the Hugging Face Incident, in which OpenAI’s AI agents breached the open-source AI community to find answers to a problem they were tasked with solving. “With the 6 Cyber model, we were able to make huge improvements on this evaluation,” Fouad Matin, the head of OpenAI’s cyber preparedness and safety team, said during a press briefing. “It’s over 99 percent of the time doing what you ask.”
But evaluation awareness, or when an AI system recognizes that it’s being tested and changes its behavior in response, remains a concern. “Evaluation awareness is super top of mind for us,” Matin said. “Often when we do see evaluation awareness, you’ll see it in the model’s chain of thought.” Matin added that OpenAI is trying to prioritize production-like evaluations, where the model is interacting with real codebases with a real objective to lessen the risk of awareness.
Following a wave of AI cybersecurity incidents, OpenAI has raced to strengthen its safeguards and lock down its most powerful models. The company briefly paused training of its frontier AI models, and it now restricts their access to the internet.
GPT-6 Cyber is classified as Critical in cybersecurity on OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, which indicates that it “can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention.” GPT-5.6 Cyber was previously classified as High under the framework.
GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s flagship Critical-level model, on most cyber-related tasks. In ExploitGym, an AI benchmark that measures whether an AI model can exploit vulnerabilities, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent, about 16 points higher than GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1 percent and a few points higher than GPT-6 Astra’s 42.4 percent score. The model helped find 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox, and it played a role in hardening OpenAI’s own infrastructure for training AI models, OpenAI says.
Additionally, GPT-6 Cyber comes with stronger safeguards “to detect and disrupt misuse” while better adhering to user instructions. OpenAI says it’s using new checks to block “high-risk activity,” including attacks on critical infrastructure like power plants and water treatment facilities.
GPT-6 Cyber is rolling out to select members of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red program, which is available to companies and organizations using its models for “authorized defensive cybersecurity work.” It’s expanding GPT-6 Cyber to all Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design
Xbox Insiders can start testing the new PC app today.
Ever since Microsoft launched its Xbox Ally handheld devices last year, it was clear the Xbox PC app still needed a lot of work to feel more like an Xbox console experience on Windows. Microsoft has greatly simplified the app now, with a design that no longer feels like you’re clicking a mouse when you’re using a controller.
“The app now launches up to 60 percent faster,” says Jason Beaumont, VP of Xbox experiences. “Pages like Home, Store, and Game Pass load up to 50 percent faster, and in-app windows open up to 65 percent faster.” The Xbox PC app also has simplified navigation that should make it easier to use on a controller, and the library section now has updated filters and better ways to organize your installed games.
Microsoft has improved the social parts of the Xbox PC app, too, with friends now listed in the main page and quick buttons to start a chat or join a party. The app overall feels less like a web one now, with what appears to be a mix of native and web elements. Microsoft has also refreshed the game card UI, as well as the home and settings sections. Even the animations have been updated to make this feel more like an Xbox dashboard experience.
I’ve been using this new Xbox PC app for the past few weeks, and it’s noticeably faster on a variety of devices I own. I’ve found it’s much easier to navigate around with a controller, and the search interface no longer tries to pop up when you’re moving between sections.
This redesign does make the Game Bar interface on handhelds feel a little out of place now, though. I understand Microsoft is looking to improve that in the coming months, and there should be design updates to make it match more closely to this updated Xbox PC app.
This new UI is also coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming. “We’re also bringing the refreshed Xbox web experience to more players and rolling out updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets,” says Beaumont. “These changes are part of our work to make Xbox faster, simpler, and more familiar wherever you play.”
The refreshed web version of Xbox Cloud Gaming has a similar look and feel to the Xbox PC app. A new library tab highlights cloud games across your own library and Xbox Game Pass. A desktop mode makes better use of larger displays, and you can choose between dark and light modes, as well as five new high-contrast options designed to improve accessibility support.
A similar design will also be available on smart TVs and VR headsets soon, but these designs aren’t exactly the same across PC, web, and smart TVs as Microsoft has customized them. “Playing on a PC, TV, or VR headset is different, and each experience needs to work well for the screen you’re using,” says Beaumont. “Wherever you play, the basics should feel familiar: finding your games, knowing what you can play, and getting into a game quickly.”

Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings (apnews.com) 73
			
		 	
				Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday amid mass protests and impeachment threats following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital lender with close ties to his administration and more than 60% of the country's adults as customers. Regulators seized the bank after uncovering risky insider lending and accounting irregularities that left its capital below legal requirements, locking millions of customers out of their savings. The Associated Press reports:  Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies. Pena repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left. Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.  Officials say they had begun repaying depositors and opening accounts at other banks for the roughly 280,000 customers who had banked exclusively with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Pena's request.
Meanwhile, eight senior Ueno executives have been detained, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. "Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud," reports the AP.

Window Sweaters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
16:50:14 UTC
01:50:14 KST

A little Mac app I made to give my windows sweaters. 🧶 Knitted borders, colours inspired by your favourite apps, and a cosier desktop.
window-sweaters-demo-github.mp4
See Window Sweaters in action on X →
You can just send this repo to your coding agent and ask it to install Window Sweaters for you:
Install Window Sweaters on my Mac: https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters
Or install it yourself with Homebrew:
brew trust saragordic/tap
brew install --cask saragordic/tap/window-sweaters
Then open Window Sweaters from your Applications folder.
You can also grab the latest ZIP from Releases, unzip it, and drag Window Sweaters.app into Applications.
If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway after trying to launch it. The app isn't notarized by Apple yet. Apple's instructions explain this step.
Click the yarn icon in your menu bar to change the style, pattern, border width, and stitch size. You can also pause the sweaters or quit from there.
To leave an app bare, open Apps and untick it. Its windows lose their sweater straight away, everything else stays as it is, and it stays off until you tick it again, even after a restart. Only want sweaters on a few apps? Choose Turn Off for All Apps, then tick the ones you like. Apps you open later start off too.
By App gives each app its own sweater. Zigzag gives them all a softer, matching cream zigzag in colours taken from their icons. Try both and see what you like.
If macOS asks for Accessibility access, enable Window Sweaters in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility so it can follow which window is focused.
Custom sweaters for 37 apps, and counting! Almost 40 little colourways, with colours picked by hand. These are just a few of my favourites:
Shown above in By App and Zigzag. Here’s everyone we’ve knitted for so far:
- Apple: Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, Notes, Calendar, Reminders, Apple Music, Photos, Preview, Terminal.
- Work and notes: Notion, Paper, Granola, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom.
- Coding and AI: Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok Bot, Ghostty.
- Design: Figma, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator.
- Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook.
- More favourites: Spotify, WhatsApp, Google Chrome, Firefox, Telegram, Discord.
See every sweater and its close-up stitches in the catalogue, or download the By App PDF.
The 37 custom sweaters keep their hand-picked colours and patterns. Other apps borrow colours from their own icons, softened into yarn, and get a two-colour zigzag, picnic or twinkle sweater in By App mode. The pattern stays the same for each app. If an icon has no usable colour, the app keeps a stable colour chosen from its name.
Icons are sampled locally in the background when needed. While the colour is being prepared, the border uses its usual fallback. Zigzag uses icon colours for every app, the 37 custom ones included, with a cream zigzag, or a deeper shade of the app’s colour on pale apps. Colours you set in apps.conf always win. Other shared patterns keep their own contrast yarns, with each app’s own base colour.
I built this on my Mac and use it myself, but there are still rough edges. Borders hide while you resize a window and return when you're done.
The app is built for macOS 13 or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel. I've tested it on Apple Silicon with macOS 26; older macOS versions and Intel Macs haven't had the same hands-on testing. It uses private macOS window APIs, so system updates may affect how it works.
If something looks wrong, open an issue and tell me your macOS version, Mac model, and whether you're using another screen. Reproduction steps help a lot.
You'll need Apple's Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) and Python 3.
git clone https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters.git
cd window-sweaters
./scripts/build-app.sh
python3 scripts/install-local.py
This builds outputs/Window Sweaters.app, installs it in ~/Applications, and opens it. The installer backs up any previous local installation before replacing it.
If you'd like to experiment, edit these files and restart the app:
~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/apps.conf
~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/charts/
The folder still uses the app's original name so existing settings keep working. For example, an app rule looks like this:
Claude = #D58561 atelier-claude
Names match app-name prefixes, ignoring capitalisation; the longest match wins. You can also put your own PNG charts in the charts folder to replace built-in patterns.
If you like setting things up from the command line, Window Sweaters also runs an optional shell script at startup, if you have one at ~/.config/window-sweaters/sweatersrc or ~/.sweatersrc.
Quit Window Sweaters from the yarn icon first. Then, if you installed it with Homebrew:
brew uninstall --zap --cask window-sweaters
--zap also removes your saved colourways. Leave it off to keep them for later.
If you installed it by hand, drag Window Sweaters.app to the Trash, then delete these if you want everything gone:
~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders
~/Library/Preferences/local.knitborders.app.plist
macOS remembers the Accessibility permission separately, so remove Window Sweaters from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility too.
make test       # run the tests
make catalogue  # render the sweater collection
make bench     # benchmark the renderer
See CONTRIBUTING.md for more details.
Built on JankyBorders by Felix Kratz, with thanks. Released under GPL-3.0. See NOTICE.md for attribution.

Working with an AI assistant collapses into a few moves you repeat all day: send a prompt, speak the next one, approve what came back, or throw it out and go again. The F4 gives each move its own key with an icon cap to match, so the loop runs through your fingers, not through menus.
Off the clock, the same four keys handle whatever you repeat most: copy/paste, meeting mute, window snapping, or a macro chain.
Start voice input with a tap. Talk through a feature idea or describe what went wrong while it’s still fresh in your mind.
Turn the prompts you use most into one-press shortcuts. Ask AI to review a code change for bugs without typing out the same request again.
One fixed ball position can't fit every hand. With T1 HE, adjust the 34 mm trackball to match your hand size, thumb reach, and grip — less awkward stretching, less unnecessary tension, and a much easier adjustment for trackball newcomers. The ball is also removable, making routine cleaning quick and easy.
Thanks to Dynamic Keystrokes (DKS), you can now assign up to 4 distinct actions per key based on press depth. A light press moves your character, a deeper press makes them run, and releasing the key enables additional commands. This layered control lets you execute multiple moves with ease.
Plug in, open launcher in your browser, and the F4 is ready to configure — no download, no driver. Choose a ready-made preset for Codex or Claude and go, or remap the keys, record macros, and set how far each key travels.
The Codex and Claude presets each include a key for voice input. Prefer to just say it? The built-in AI assistant sets keys up from a plain-language request.
*The F4 does not have a built-in microphone. For voice input, use your computer's built-in microphone or an external microphone.

Map the keys to your in-game moves, such as weapon swaps, abilities, push-to-talk, and tune how deep each press registers. Magnetic switches and wired 8,000 Hz polling keep every action responsive.
The F4 HE 8K comes with pre-lubed Keychron Ultra-Fast Lime Magnetic Switches for smooth, stable keystrokes. These switches also let you set each key's actuation point from 0.20 to 3.30 mm with 0.1 mm sensitivity. Choose a shallower setting to register a press sooner or a deeper setting for more deliberate input.
With a wired polling rate of 8,000 Hz, the F4 HE 8K can report key inputs to your computer up to 8,000 times per second. It delivers responsive input whether you’re running a shortcut at work or switching weapons mid-match. Pair it with an 8K-rated cable like the Keychron Coiled Aviator Cable 8K since standard USB-C cables cap the polling rate.
*8,000 Hz polling requires a USB-C cable that supports an 8K polling rate.
Need a break? The F4 taps like a fidget piece — smooth keystrokes, soft sound. And at 44.94 mm square with a lanyard, it leaves the desk as easily as it lives on it: clip it to your bag and take your shortcuts along.

Where is Windows 12?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
16:29:41 UTC
01:29:41 KST

While I wasn’t expecting Microsoft to announce Windows 12 during its RTX Spark launch event last month, more than a few people were hoping to see something truly new. Between the growing frustration with Windows 11 and the muted response to Copilot Plus PCs, it’s starting to feel like Microsoft needs to go bigger with its desktop OS.
Where is Windows 12?
Microsoft seems happy to stick with Windows 11, for now.
Much of this year’s Windows development has been focused on underlying performance improvements, after Microsoft acknowledged the bloat and reliability issues with Windows 11 and created a plan to fix them. That work is ongoing, and sources tell me there’s now a big focus on quality for the next major release of Windows 11 in 2027.
Microsoft started planning to shift back to a three-year release cycle for Windows in 2022, with the first big release in 2024. At the time, many expected that to be Windows 12, but the company stuck to a major update of Windows 11 instead. Now that the three-year cycle is about to hit again, it looks like Microsoft is promising to improve Windows 11 instead of rolling new features and underlying improvements into a Windows 12 release.
Sources tell me that Microsoft is already preparing for Windows 11 version 27H2. Like the big 24H2 release in 2024, this will be a full OS swap, where Microsoft replaces or upgrades major parts of the OS. The past couple of annual releases (25H2 and 26H2) have been enablement packages, which simply switch new features on gradually as they’re rolled out in monthly cumulative updates.
Since this is a bigger release, more testing will be required for the new features and changes that Microsoft is planning to make next year. We will likely see Windows Insider testing begin a lot sooner than the typical June timeframe Microsoft used for both 25H2 and 26H2.
Microsoft is also preparing for the big release of Windows 11 next year by replacing the default wallpaper of the operating system. Sources tell me a new wallpaper will be unveiled at Microsoft’s Ignite conference later this month, with a series of designs replacing Bloom, the current default. Microsoft used Bloom to market Windows 11 heavily during its launch phase, with “Bloomberry” ice cream and the wallpaper gracing the famous Times Square screens.
The wallpaper replacements will vary across consumer and commercial versions of Windows 11, I’m told. The designs are similar to Bloom, but with a folding sheet of color immersed in clouds. The Windows 11 Pro version looks the most like the Bloom colors, while there are subtle variations for the consumer versions of Windows 11, focused on gaming, productivity, creator, and performance.
Microsoft has quietly started using some of these new wallpapers in its recent Windows 11 marketing materials, and it plans to preview the full Bloom replacement at Ignite before rolling it out broadly in early January.
The question I can’t answer yet is whether Microsoft will even consider moving to Windows 12 branding next year, or whether that’s still a few years away. Microsoft seems to be set on improving Windows 11’s reputation, but it’s a difficult task to achieve when lots of people have already made their minds up.
Even Microsoft’s performance improvements haven’t convinced everyone yet. Microsoft showed off some more of its memory optimization work earlier this week, improving performance and multitasking on PCs with 8GB of RAM. “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return,” explains Windows chief Pavan Davuluri.
I’ve seen YouTubers and even some Windows Insiders question this work, skeptical that Microsoft is actually making improvements. But it’s not just a false promise from Windows engineers; there’s a big effort to make a series of small improvements that all add up to a better performance across a variety of hardware.
Windows Central tested Microsoft’s claims and found that the latest updates to Windows 11 do, in fact, improve memory usage. Paging less data to disk will also improve performance, particularly when you’re multitasking between apps on a system with just 8GB of RAM. Microsoft is making improvements to memory usage in apps like Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook, too, so this isn’t even just a Windows effort anymore.
These changes are hard to notice unless you compare two systems side by side, and Microsoft clearly has a perception problem with Windows 11 that steady improvements like this won’t overcome.
Microsoft ultimately missed a chance to simply own up to the malware-like ads it has squeezed into Windows 11 and be transparent about the fact that they were a mistake. Instead, I think the company is betting that it can win back users over the long term through genuine improvements rather than a marketing exercise that packages everything up into a shiny, new Windows 12 release. Whether that’s enough to change how people feel about Windows remains to be seen, but Microsoft needs to give people a reason to be excited about Windows again, not just another reason to tolerate it.
The pad
- The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic are all promising to adopt a new standard that will allow publishers to opt out of being scraped by AI bots. As Google Zero continues to reshape the publishing industry, Microsoft says websites will still appear in Bing’s search results even if AI training has been blocked. Anthropic has already adopted this new signal, which is part of a website’s robots.txt file, and Google and Microsoft are both planning to support it next year.
- Curry Barker used a Surface Laptop Ultra to help make his new YouTube short. Microsoft is promoting the performance benefits of RTX Spark on battery by showcasing that Obsession director Curry Barker used a Surface Laptop Ultra to edit the full Mama Bear film while unplugged. The edit obviously wasn’t performed on a single battery charge, as Microsoft notes, but it’s more to point out that Windows laptops have finally caught up to the MacBook Pro’s ability to maintain near-identical performance whether on battery or plugged in.
- Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search. Microsoft has started testing new Windows 11 builds that improve on the recently refreshed Windows Search and add quick settings to Xbox mode. Windows Insiders can now test out filters in search for files, actions, or web results, as well as perform actions like changing screen brightness or volume. The Xbox mode in Windows 11 is also getting quick settings to easily toggle things like Bluetooth and Wi-Fi without having to exit to the desktop mode on a handheld gaming PC.
- Xbox’s former COO has “serious concerns” about her abrupt departure. I said this was weird last week. Xbox’s former chief operating officer, Helen Chiang, suddenly left Microsoft less than two weeks ago after being promoted into the role in July. A surprisingly short memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed the news internally, and now Chiang says she has “serious concerns” about how she was treated. In a lengthy post on LinkedIn, Chiang doesn’t dispute she was fired but says a Eurogamer report that it was related to policy violations is “not accurate.” Chiang also denies unfounded rumors that speculated she was leaking information, or that she left to join a competitor. I’ve only heard really positive things about Chiang, so this whole turn of events is very puzzling.
- The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel. I reported in Notepad last week that Sentinel would be the official subtitle of The Elder Scrolls VI, and Bethesda confirmed it this week with a brief teaser video. While the game is still at least two years away from release, Bethesda has been showing off some parts of the story internally in recent months. There have been many leaks about The Elder Scrolls VI in recent years, and I will say that one was very accurate, while many others have been far off the mark.
- Xbox’s smallest-ever controller is surprisingly comfortable. I’ve been testing out the new $49.99 Xbox Nano controller over the past few days, and I’m impressed with the design. I have small hands so it’s perfectly suited to me, and it’s designed for younger people and gaming on the go. The big difference with the Nano over regular Xbox controllers is the size of the triggers. They’re also a lot more clicky than the thud on the regular controller. The battery life is also something you’ll have to get used to, as it seems to drain fully in around five to six hours.
- Xbox’s Arkane Studios attracts multiple bidders, including Ubisoft. We’re just weeks away from hearing about the fate of Blade developers Arkane Studios, and it looks like Microsoft has some options lined up for the studio. Bloomberg reports that Ubisoft and “at least two other gaming companies” have made bids for Arkane. Microsoft is also considering selling the studio to its management. I wrote last week that “I’m cautiously optimistic that Blade will be saved.”
- Microsoft is improving Outlook search with a small language model. Microsoft has heard the feedback about Outlook search and it’s looking to improve result ranking, results when connectivity is poor, and a better feedback loop for end users. Classic Outlook will now automatically fall back to a local index when connectivity to cloud servers is poor. This should improve the speed of results, but Microsoft is also using an Outlook-specific small language model ranker to improve the relevancy and speed of results. You’ll also be able to use a thumbs up or down on Outlook search results to let Microsoft know how happy you are with the changes.
- The new Windows 11 speed test was built by an AI agent. Microsoft saw the feedback about the taskbar speed test throwing you to a webpage, and it designed a fully integrated version for Windows 11 instead. “The design and build work was driven by an agentic AI workflow, with a person guiding the process in their spare time,” says Marcus Ash, head of design and research for Windows and devices. It took only a day to get a working prototype ready. “This is where I see a lot of potential in AI,” says Ash. “Getting from idea to customer value faster. Without AI slop. That is the way.”
- Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games. Microsoft’s new Xbox Nano controller now supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, just like Google’s Stadia controllers. It was a hidden feature when I tried out the new controller recently, and US players will be able to preview it ahead of a broader rollout. Microsoft is also previewing a new phone controller option for playing cloud games on smart TVs.
- Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design. Microsoft is unveiling a new Xbox PC app today that launches “up to 60 percent faster” than before, with an overhauled design to match new updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and smart TVs. Xbox Insiders will be able to start testing the updated Xbox PC app today, and the updated Xbox Cloud Gaming interface will start rolling out over the next few weeks. I’ve been trying out the new Xbox PC app on the Xbox Ally X handheld in recent weeks, and it’s noticeably faster and feels much more like I’m navigating an Xbox console interface than before. It’s good to see these much-needed improvements for the Xbox PC app.

The Stacks Project, Formalized in Lean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
16:16:59 UTC
01:16:59 KST

Today, Axiom is releasing our Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project, the roughly 7,500-page open-source reference that lays the foundations of modern algebraic geometry. Spanning some 16 million lines of code, it is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built.
With this release, the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project is available as a single, machine-checked library. Researchers and AI agents alike can import its definitions and theorems directly into new formal proofs, while permanent Stacks tags link every Lean declaration back to the canonical text mathematicians already know.
This milestone begins with the Stacks Project itself. Initiated by Columbia University mathematician Johan de Jong in 2005, it has grown through the tireless work of hundreds of mathematicians who have contributed proofs, examples, and refinements over two decades. Our formalization rests equally on the foundations of the Lean and Mathlib communities. Formalizing a corpus of this magnitude was only possible because those communities spent years building a rich mathematical library, along with the abstractions needed to organize it, long before our work began.
Why formalize a foundational reference of this scale? As AI systems begin generating mathematical arguments at a pace far beyond what humans can inspect by hand, formal verification becomes essential. In fields with mature Lean infrastructure, new results can often be formalized shortly after they are discovered. Until now, modern algebraic geometry has been far harder to approach this way: a single contemporary proof may invoke a long chain of theorems across commutative algebra, schemes, sheaves, cohomology, and algebraic stacks before its core argument even begins. The mathematics existed in the Stacks Project, but the corresponding Lean infrastructure did not.
Closing that gap is as much a software engineering challenge as a mathematical one. While uncoordinated AI code generation can produce short, isolated scripts quickly, scaling to millions of lines of verified mathematics requires clean abstractions, stable interfaces, and components that fit together across an entire codebase. To achieve this, we deployed coordinated swarms of AI agents capable of translating, proving, and integrating thousands of theorems in parallel. Formalizing the Stacks Project in its entirety establishes a new starting point for algebraic geometry and the many neighboring fields that rely on its machinery.
The mathematics behind Stacks
At its heart, algebraic geometry studies the interplay between algebraic equations and the geometric shapes they describe. Over the real numbers, the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ defines a circle; over the rational numbers, its points correspond to Pythagorean triples, such as $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$. Studying the same equations across different number systems, or in families that vary over a parameter space, connects geometry directly to number theory and algebra. These ideas also reach beyond pure mathematics: elliptic curves secure modern digital cryptography, while algebraic curves over finite fields power error-correcting codes. Modern algebraic geometry provides a common language for studying equations across all of these settings.
Forging that language took generations. Emmy Noether revolutionized algebra by shifting focus from individual equations to abstract structures such as rings, modules, and ideals. Just as the right software abstraction can replace thousands of special-purpose routines with a single reusable framework, a theorem proved for the right algebraic structure applies across many concrete settings at once. A generation later, Alexander Grothendieck and his collaborators introduced the theory of schemes, creating a sweeping dictionary between algebra and geometry that allowed mathematicians to do geometry over arbitrary rings, with arithmetic and infinitesimal data built in from the start. Monumental treatises like Éléments de géométrie algébrique (EGA) and Séminaire de géométrie algébrique du Bois Marie (SGA) rebuilt the foundations of the discipline from the ground up, supplying the machinery behind landmark breakthroughs including Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures and Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
Yet as the subject expanded, its foundational literature grew vast, scattered across thousands of pages of dense monographs and seminars, much of it written in French. A great deal of the subject's working knowledge also lived as unwritten folklore passed down from advisor to student. Even defining an algebraic stack, a geometric space capable of remembering the internal symmetries of the objects it parametrizes, requires a formidable tower of prerequisites spanning commutative algebra, topologies, sheaves, and cohomology. Mathematicians needed a unified, self-contained reference where those prerequisites were written down in full detail.
In 2005, de Jong set out to organize those foundations the way software engineers maintain an open-source project like the Linux kernel. What began as an accessible introduction to algebraic stacks evolved into a living, collaborative encyclopedia comprising thousands of permanent four-character tags. The Stacks Project operates on rigorous editorial principles: every theorem carries a proof, every assumption is stated explicitly, and every step points back to the exact tags on which it depends. In doing so, de Jong and his collaborators anticipated the architecture of formal proof libraries, demonstrating that mathematics becomes far easier to verify and extend when its components have stable identifiers and explicit dependency graphs. Translating the Stacks Project into Lean brings mechanical verification to that human-designed architecture.
A library built for reuse
On October 27, 2026, Axiom released our Lean formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG). While CFSG and the Stacks Project are both monumental in scale, they represent fundamentally different engineering challenges. CFSG is organized around a single landmark theorem. The Stacks Project, by contrast, is a foundational library: its value lies in thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas designed to be reused across countless future proofs.
With this library, a mathematician or AI agent formalizing a new theorem about families of curves no longer needs to reconstruct the foundations of schemes or coherent cohomology from scratch. They can import the relevant definitions and theorems directly, while Lean’s kernel guarantees that every cited result is applied only when its exact hypotheses are satisfied. Formalizing the Stacks Project as one connected codebase gives researchers and agents a common chain of verified definitions and theorems on which to build, something no collection of isolated proof scripts can provide.
To make our library easy to navigate, our release preserves the permanent tag structure of the original text. At stacks.axiommath.ai, readers can view the pages of the original Stacks Project side-by-side with the corresponding Lean code and explore the interactive dependency graph. Because a single Stacks tag often unfolds into multiple formal definitions and lemmas, some newly defined and others bridged directly to existing declarations in Mathlib, our interface tracks these mappings explicitly so researchers can see precisely how the informal and formal developments align.
Engineering coherent mathematics at scale
A smorgasbord of independently verified proofs does not make a usable mathematical library. If thousands of AI agents formalize theorems in parallel without architectural coordination, two agents will inevitably prove correct theorems about the same mathematical object using subtly incompatible definitions, or duplicate foundational infrastructure that already exists in Mathlib. Lean’s kernel will accept both files in isolation, but their results will be painfully difficult to compose downstream. Building coherent formal infrastructure requires keeping every definition and interface aligned across the entire project.
At this scale, formalization is as much systems engineering as it is mathematics. To build a single, unified library, our mathematicians and engineers designed a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities and strict coordination protocols. Agents worked in parallel across the dependency graph to translate statements, search Mathlib for existing abstractions, construct proofs, and resolve prerequisites, all while keeping definitions, typeclass interfaces, and mathematical abstractions aligned across chapters.
In a tightly interconnected dependency graph of definitions and theorems, an unfaithful or trivialized formalization is quickly exposed. Ensuring that each formal statement faithfully captures the mathematical meaning of the original text is even more important than verifying its proof. Across the library, statement faithfulness is enforced automatically at scale through multi-agent auditing, semantic cross-checks against the source text, and the strict requirement that every definition and lemma must successfully interface with the downstream theorems that depend on it. Combined with targeted audits on foundational definitions and landmark theorems, this automated verification pipeline ensures that the formal library remains faithful to the mathematics of the Stacks Project.
What formal verification reveals
Over the course of the project, our system surfaced dozens of statements in the Stacks Project that required local refinement, including missing hypotheses, edge cases in positive characteristic, and claims that did not hold in the full generality stated. Rather than treating failed proof attempts as mere obstacles, our agents diagnosed the underlying mathematical obstructions and constructed explicit counterexamples to prove where the original statements broke down.
Once an obstruction was isolated, the system worked to repair the mathematics so downstream chapters could still depend on it. For local oversights, our agents identified the exact missing hypotheses and formalized the corrected theorems alongside their counterexamples. Where a false supporting lemma created a gap in the proof of a deeper theorem, the agents found alternative routes through the literature to establish the main result under its original hypotheses. Together, these resolutions show how large-scale formalization can actively refine and strengthen the mathematical literature itself.
A monument to the past, a foundation for the future
Ultimately, the mathematics inside this library is the product of generations of human creativity, from the geometric intuition of the early pioneers, to the structural revolutions of Noether and Grothendieck, to the open-source scholarship of the Stacks Project and Mathlib communities. Each generation inherited a body of mathematical knowledge, cast it into a sharper language, and handed the next generation a stronger foundation. We see this formalization as part of that ongoing tradition: both a tribute to the mathematicians who built modern algebraic geometry, and working infrastructure for an emerging era in which humans and AI agents explore new mathematical frontiers together.
In an October 21, 2026 announcement, de Jong requested that AI-generated comments and pull requests not be submitted directly to the upstream Stacks Project repository for the time being. The Stacks Project remains an active, living text under the stewardship of Johan de Jong and its community of contributors, while this Lean formalization is an independent open-source project maintained by Axiom. We fully respect that boundary: we keep our formalization, counterexamples, and refinements in our own repository, where mathematicians can review and draw upon them on their own terms.
You can explore the side-by-side text, inspect counterexamples, and trace the full dependency graph at stacks.axiommath.ai. Like the Stacks Project itself, our formalization is open source and designed to grow over time. We invite mathematicians, Lean developers, and AI agents to examine the library, refine its abstractions, and build new mathematics upon it.

Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
16:16:45 UTC
01:16:45 KST

It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.
Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.
On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.
Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.
The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.
Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.
Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.
For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.
That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.
“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”
The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.
“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.
To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”
Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.
The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.
Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”
Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”
Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.
Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.
“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”
The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.
“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”
Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”
